title: Design Google Drive / Dropbox
description: A cloud-based file storage and sync service supporting multi-device uploads, downloads, sharing, and real-time sync with chunked uploads, CDN delivery, and delta sync.

functional: Users can upload files up to 50GB from any device with resumable chunked uploads and progress tracking
Users can download files from any device via CDN-signed URLs for low-latency delivery
Users can share files with other users and view files shared with them via ACL-based permissions
Clients automatically sync file changes across devices using WebSocket push plus polling fallback
nonFunctional: High availability — prioritize availability over strict consistency; brief staleness is acceptable for file listings
Low latency — CDN edge caching for downloads, chunked parallel uploads, and delta sync for file changes
Reliability — files replicated across multiple zones; metadata backed up with operation logs
Scalability — support millions of users, petabytes of storage, and thousands of concurrent uploads/downloads

estimates.label: Daily active users
estimates.note: each syncing ~50 files per day across multiple devices

estimates.label: Storage volume
estimates.note: average 100GB per active user with deduplication reducing raw storage

estimates.label: Peak upload rate
estimates.note: chunked into 5-10MB parts with multipart upload to object storage

estimates.label: Read : write ratio
estimates.note: downloads and sync checks dwarf uploads — CDN absorbs most read traffic

estimates.label: Sync latency target
estimates.note: WebSocket push for active clients, polling fallback every few minutes

stages.title: The MVP — direct uploads to object storage
stages.narrative:
The simplest version: a client discovers the service via DNS, authenticates through an API Gateway and Auth Service, and uploads/downloads files through the File Service — which generates presigned URLs so file bytes flow directly to and from object storage.

Metadata (file name, size, fingerprint) is persisted in a DynamoDB table keyed by userId. This works for thousands of users, but every download comes from a single regional bucket — latency is high for global users and origin egress costs grow linearly.

stages.title: Add the CDN for global downloads
stages.trigger: Users far from the origin region wait 200ms+ for every download, and origin egress costs dominate the infrastructure budget
stages.narrative:
A **CDN** now fronts object storage for downloads: DNS geo-routes to the nearest edge, and cache hits serve in <20ms. Signed URLs with short expiration (5 minutes) enforce access control at the edge.

The CDN also supports **Range requests** so interrupted downloads resume without restarting — critical for mobile networks. Popular files are cached globally; the long tail still streams from origin.

stages.title: Add real-time sync across devices
stages.trigger: Users with multiple devices expect file edits on their laptop to appear on their phone within seconds — polling is too slow and too expensive at 100M DAU
stages.narrative:
A **Sync Service** maintains WebSocket connections per device for near-real-time push. When a file changes, the File Service publishes a **file.changes** event to a Kafka event bus. The **Notification Worker** consumes the event and pushes a sync notification through the **WebSocket Manager** to all of the user's online devices.

A **Shared Files Cache** (Redis) sits in front of the metadata DB to accelerate ACL lookups for frequently shared files. Offline devices get changes via periodic polling (GET /files/changes?since=...) when they reconnect.

stages.title: Add sharing and email notifications
stages.trigger: File sharing is the primary growth vector — users need to share files and invite collaborators via email
stages.narrative:
The system reaches its full shape. An **Email Provider** sends share-invite notifications when a user shares a file with someone who doesn't yet have an account.

The Notification Worker also forwards events to the Email Provider asynchronously, keeping the sharing path decoupled from the notification delivery. This is the finished architecture: every tier — upload, download, sync, share — is decoupled by the event bus, and each scales independently.

nodes.name: Web Client
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Chunk files into 5-10MB parts using Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) for delta sync
- Compress files client-side before upload (zstd for text, skip for media)
- Upload chunks directly to object storage via presigned URLs
- Download files via CDN-signed URLs with Range request support for resumable downloads
- Monitor local filesystem for changes and sync via WebSocket + polling fallback

nodes.name: Mobile App
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Same chunking and compression logic as desktop
- Background sync with OS-constrained network usage
- Offline mode with local cache and conflict resolution on reconnect

nodes.name: Desktop Client
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- FileSystemWatcher / FSEvents / inotify for real-time local change detection
- Delta sync using CDC — only re-upload chunks that changed
- Conflict resolution with last-write-wins and optional versioning hooks

nodes.name: DNS
nodes.details: Routes users to the nearest CDN edge or API gateway based on geographic location.

nodes.name: CDN (CloudFront)
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Cache frequently accessed files at 400+ edge locations worldwide
- Validate CDN-signed URLs (signature + expiration + optional IP binding)
- Serve cache hits directly; forward misses to object storage with request coalescing
- Support Range requests for partial/resumable downloads

failure.userImpact: Download latency jumps from ~20ms to 200ms+ as every request misses the cache and hits the origin S3 bucket directly. Origin egress costs explode.

blastRadius.note: absorbs the entire read load the edge used to soak
slow downloads, Range requests served from origin
slow downloads on mobile networks — resumable but painful

failure.mitigation: Files are plain HTTPS objects, so clients can fall back to direct S3 presigned URLs — degraded but alive. Real platforms run **multiple CDNs** with DNS-level failover. Request coalescing at the origin blunts the initial miss storm.

nodes.name: API Gateway
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Authenticate requests via JWT/session tokens
- Rate limit uploads/downloads per user
- Route to File Service, Sync Service, or Auth Service
- Enforce request size limits (API Gateway max ~10MB; large files bypass via presigned URLs)

nodes.name: Auth Service
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Issue and validate JWT access tokens
- Handle OAuth 2.0 / SSO login flows
- Manage refresh token rotation and revocation

nodes.name: File Service
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- CRUD operations on file metadata (name, size, MIME type, fingerprint, chunk status)
- Generate S3 presigned URLs for multipart upload parts (purely local crypto operation)
- Generate CDN-signed URLs for downloads with short expiration (e.g., 5 min)
- Verify chunk uploads via S3 ListParts API before marking chunks as uploaded
- Call S3 CompleteMultipartUpload once all chunks are verified
- Enforce ACLs via SharedFiles table lookups

failure.userImpact: Uploads and downloads fail — users cannot list, upload, or download files. Any files already cached at the CDN edge remain accessible via their signed URLs until they expire.

blastRadius.note: file routes return errors; auth and sync routes still work
no reads or writes reaching it from the file path
no new file.change events published

failure.mitigation: The File Service is **stateless** — health checks eject bad instances and autoscaling replaces them. The CDN continues serving cached files; only metadata operations are affected.

nodes.name: Sync Service
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Maintain WebSocket connections per device for real-time push
- Publish change events (create/update/delete) to connected clients
- Handle GET /files/changes?since={timestamp} for polling fallback
- Coordinate delta sync by comparing client and server chunk fingerprints

failure.userImpact: Real-time sync stops working — file changes no longer propagate instantly. The polling fallback (every few minutes) still catches changes, so no data is lost, only delayed.

blastRadius.note: no subscriptions to manage or push through
sync events still published by File Service but no consumer from sync path

failure.mitigation: The Sync Service is **stateless** — it restarts and re-establishes WebSocket connections. During the outage, the polling fallback (GET /files/changes?since=...) guarantees eventual consistency.

nodes.name: Notification Worker
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Consume file change events from Kafka
- Push WebSocket notifications to relevant user devices
- Update search index and shared file caches asynchronously

failure.userImpact: Real-time push notifications stop — newly uploaded files or edits on one device do not appear on others until they manually refresh or the polling interval fires.

blastRadius.note: events accumulate; consumer offset lag grows
no events forwarded; no push notifications sent
share-invite emails not sent until worker recovers

failure.mitigation: The worker is **stateless** and resumes from its last Kafka offset. Events buffer in Kafka during the outage — nothing is lost, only delayed until the worker drains the backlog.

nodes.name: File Metadata DB
nodes.details:
### Schema

**FileMetadata table:**
- Partition Key: `userId`
- Sort Key: `fileId`
- Attributes: name, size, mimeType, fingerprint, status (uploading/uploaded), chunks[], createdAt, updatedAt

**SharedFiles table:**
- Partition Key: `userId` (who the file is shared with)
- Sort Key: `fileId`
- Enables fast lookup of all files shared with a given user without full table scans

failure.userImpact: File listing, upload status checks, and share verification all fail. Files already cached at the CDN edge remain downloadable via existing signed URLs until they expire.

blastRadius.note: cannot read or write metadata — all file operations fail
session and user lookups depend on this store
entries expire with nowhere to refill from

failure.mitigation: DynamoDB is a **managed, replicated store** — individual partition failures are rare. The shared-cache (Redis) continues serving cached ACLs for its TTL window, softening the blow for read-heavy share lookups.

nodes.name: Shared Files Cache
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Cache userId -> fileId[] mappings for shared files
- TTL of 5 minutes with cache-aside pattern
- Reduces DynamoDB read load for frequent share list queries

nodes.name: WebSocket Manager
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Maintain persistent WebSocket connections per active device
- Subscribe to per-user Kafka topics for real-time change push
- Handle connection drops with exponential backoff reconnection

failure.userImpact: Real-time push notifications stop reaching active devices. The app appears to be in sync but silently misses updates until the user manually refreshes or the polling interval fires.

blastRadius.note: WebSocket subscriptions are lost; no push path available
events still processed but cannot reach connected clients

failure.mitigation: Clients detect the WebSocket drop and reconnect with exponential backoff. The polling fallback (GET /files/changes) guarantees eventual consistency during the gap, and a fresh WebSocket connection resumes real-time delivery on reconnect.

nodes.name: Object Storage (S3)
nodes.description: Blob storage for file chunks & objects
nodes.details:
### Responsibilities

- Store file chunks and assembled objects with 3x cross-zone replication
- Support multipart upload API (CreateMultipartUpload, UploadPart, CompleteMultipartUpload, ListParts, AbortMultipartUpload)
- Server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) for data at rest
- Lifecycle policies to transition old versions to cheaper storage classes
- Event notifications on CompleteMultipartUpload to trigger metadata updates

failure.userImpact: Uploads and downloads break entirely — new files cannot be stored and existing files cannot be served. The CDN edge cache continues serving files that were already cached, but any miss is fatal.

blastRadius.note: cache misses cannot fetch from origin; only cached files remain available
cannot issue presigned URLs or verify uploads

failure.mitigation: S3 stores data across **multiple Availability Zones** with 11 9s of durability. A regional outage is the only realistic failure mode, mitigated by cross-region replication for critical user data.

nodes.name: Event Bus (Kafka)
nodes.details:
### Topics

- `file.changes` — file create/update/delete events
- `sync.notifications` — per-user device notification events
- `search.index` — search index update events
- `analytics.events` — usage metrics and billing events

failure.userImpact: Real-time sync and notifications stop — file changes still happen but are not propagated to other devices until the queue recovers. Uploads and downloads continue unaffected.

blastRadius.note: no events to consume — push pipeline stalls
sync events buffer at the producer; reconnect drains the backlog

failure.mitigation: Kafka is **replicated across brokers** and survives individual node failures. Producers buffer events in-memory during brief outages; a reconciliation job can re-enqueue missed events by scanning recent file modifications.

nodes.name: Email Provider
nodes.details: Sends email invitations when users share files with others who don't yet have accounts.

flows.title: Upload a Large File
flows.description: From selecting a file to it being available for download, with chunked resumable upload.

steps.text: The desktop client detects a new file via FileSystemWatcher, chunks it using Content-Defined Chunking (CDC), and computes SHA-256 fingerprints for deduplication.

stateChanges.note: file chunked into 240 CDC parts; fingerprints computed

steps.text: The client requests a presigned multipart upload URL from the File Service via the API Gateway. The File Service creates a multipart upload in S3 and returns presigned URLs for each chunk.
The client uploads chunks directly to S3 using the presigned URLs, bypassing our backend entirely. Multiple chunks are uploaded in parallel to maximize bandwidth.

payload.title: PUT {presigned-url} · part 42 / 240
payload.body:
Content-Length: 5242880
x-amz-part-number: 42

‹ 5 MB chunk of CDC-partitioned file ›

stateChanges.note: 41/240 parts landed; failed chunks retry alone, never the whole file

steps.text: After each chunk upload, the client sends chunk status + ETag to the File Service. The service verifies via S3 ListParts API before updating the metadata DB.

stateChanges.note: chunk 42/240 marked as uploaded; status = uploading

steps.text: Once all chunks are verified, the File Service calls S3 CompleteMultipartUpload to assemble the object, then marks the file as 'uploaded' in the metadata DB.

stateChanges.note: object assembled from 240 parts in S3
status = uploaded; file is now readable

steps.text: The File Service publishes a 'file.changes' event to Kafka. The Notification Worker consumes it and pushes a sync notification via WebSocket to all of the user's other devices.

stateChanges.note: event published — Notification Worker drains asynchronously
WebSocket push sent to all active devices

flows.title: Download a Shared File
flows.description: From requesting a file to receiving it via the nearest CDN edge.

steps.text: The mobile app requests to download a file. The request goes through DNS geo-routing to the API Gateway, which authenticates the user.

payload.title: GET /api/files/report.pdf?action=download
payload.body:
→ Auth: JWT validated
→ Route to File Service

steps.text: The File Service checks the SharedFiles table and cache to verify the user has access, then generates a CDN-signed URL with a 5-minute expiration.

payload.title: ACL check + sign URL
payload.body:
→ DynamoDB Query(SharedFiles, userId = mobile_user)
→ HIT: user has access
→ Sign: CloudFront URL (expires in 300s)

stateChanges.note: ACL cache hit — permission verified in <2ms

steps.text: The client downloads the file directly from the nearest CDN edge. On a cache hit, the CDN serves immediately. On a miss, it fetches from S3 with request coalescing.

stateChanges.note: cache miss → fetch from S3 → cache → serve; subsequent requests are edge hits

flows.title: Sync File Changes Across Devices
flows.description: How a file edit on desktop propagates to mobile in near real-time.

steps.text: The desktop client detects a local file change via FSEvents. It re-chunks using CDC, identifies only the changed chunks, and uploads those delta chunks to S3.

payload.title: Detect change → CDC delta
payload.body:
file: "report.pdf"
changed regions: 2 chunks (9MB total)
uploading delta to S3

stateChanges.note: 2 of 240 chunks changed; only delta chunks re-uploaded

steps.text: The File Service updates the metadata DB with new chunk fingerprints and publishes a change event to Kafka.

payload.title: Update metadata + publish event
payload.body:
UPDATE file:report.pdf SET chunks[42].fingerprint = 'sha256:f6e5d4c3b2a1…'
→ Kafka file.changes: { event: 'file.updated', userId: 'user:xyz' }

stateChanges.note: chunk fingerprints updated for delta sync

steps.text: The Notification Worker consumes the event from Kafka and pushes a real-time notification through the WebSocket Manager to the user's mobile device.

stateChanges.note: real-time push delivered to mobile device via WebSocket

steps.text: The mobile app receives the push, queries GET /files/changes?since={lastSync}, and downloads only the changed chunks via CDN-signed URLs.

payload.title: GET /api/files/changes?since=2026-07-10T11:59:00Z
payload.body:
→ [file:report.pdf (version 2)]
→ CDN-signed URL for delta chunk download

stateChanges.note: delta chunks downloaded — local file updated via CDC reassembly

decisions.title: Direct client-to-storage upload vs proxy through backend
decisions.choice: Presigned URLs + multipart upload directly to S3
alternatives: Proxy uploads through File Service servers
decisions.rationale: Video and document ingress is measured in petabytes. If file bytes flowed through our API servers, the compute tier would have to scale with *storage traffic* instead of *request traffic* — a 1000x difference. Presigned URLs let clients upload directly to S3 while our backend only handles lightweight metadata and URL generation. This pattern also enables resumable chunked uploads: if a 50GB upload fails at 49GB, only the remaining chunks need retrying.

decisions.title: Chunk boundary strategy for delta sync
decisions.rationale: Fixed-size chunks shift all boundaries when a byte is inserted at the start, causing every subsequent chunk to get a new fingerprint and forcing a full re-upload. CDC uses a rolling hash to find chunk boundaries based on *content*, so a small edit only affects 2-3 surrounding chunks. This is how Dropbox achieves efficient delta sync in practice — a 1-byte edit in a 1GB file might only re-upload ~10MB instead of 1GB.

decisions.title: Real-time sync notification mechanism
decisions.choice: WebSocket push with periodic polling fallback
decisions.rationale: WebSockets provide sub-second sync latency when devices are online, which is critical for the 'it just works' Dropbox experience. However, connections drop on mobile networks and sleep modes. A periodic poll every few minutes via GET /files/changes?since={timestamp} acts as a safety net to guarantee eventual consistency. We avoid SSE because we need bidirectional communication for the client to acknowledge sync state.

decisions.title: Sharing permission data model
decisions.rationale: An embedded sharelist requires scanning every file's metadata to find files shared with a given user — O(N) where N is total files. A normalized SharedFiles table with userId as partition key and fileId as sort key turns this into a single efficient query. We keep a Redis cache in front for hot lookups. This trades a slightly more complex write path (updating two tables in a transaction) for a dramatically faster read path.

decisions.title: Download delivery optimization
decisions.choice: CDN with signed URLs and Range request support
alternatives: Direct S3 presigned URLs without CDN
decisions.rationale: Users are globally distributed but S3 buckets are regional. A user in Sydney downloading from a US-East bucket faces 200ms+ latency per request. A CDN caches files at 400+ edge locations, reducing latency to <20ms for popular content. Signed URLs enforce that only authorized users can access cached content. Range requests let clients resume interrupted downloads without restarting — critical for mobile networks with intermittent connectivity.

bottlenecks.title: Viral file thundering herd
bottlenecks.problem: A shared folder with a popular file (e.g., a leaked document) receives millions of download requests simultaneously. The CDN origin (S3) and the File Service's metadata DB face a synchronized stampede.
bottlenecks.mitigation: The CDN absorbs 99%+ of download traffic via edge caching with request coalescing — concurrent identical cache misses collapse into a single origin fetch. The File Service caches ACL lookups in Redis with a 5-minute TTL. For truly viral events, we can temporarily increase the CDN cache TTL and serve slightly stale metadata.

bottlenecks.title: Multipart upload metadata bloat
bottlenecks.problem: Millions of concurrent large file uploads create enormous metadata state in the FileMetadata DB (chunk arrays with hundreds of entries per file). DynamoDB item size limits (400KB) can be exceeded, and query performance degrades.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Store chunk manifests in a separate ChunkManifest table with fileId as partition key, or offload to S3 itself via the ListParts API. The FileMetadata table only tracks uploadId and overall status. For files with >1000 chunks, we paginate chunk status and verify in batches via S3 ListParts rather than tracking every chunk in the DB.

bottlenecks.title: WebSocket connection exhaustion
bottlenecks.problem: With 100M DAU and an average of 2.5 devices per user, maintaining 250M persistent WebSocket connections overwhelms the Sync Service and underlying infrastructure.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a dedicated WebSocket gateway cluster (e.g., ElastiCache Redis Pub/Sub or a custom gateway) that maintains connections while the Sync Service remains stateless. Connections are sharded by userId across gateway instances. Idle connections are closed after 30 minutes; clients reconnect via polling until activity resumes.

bottlenecks.title: Duplicate storage from deduplication gaps
bottlenecks.problem: Without global deduplication, the same file uploaded by thousands of users (e.g., a popular PDF, a standard template) is stored thousands of times, wasting petabytes of storage.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Fingerprint files with SHA-256 at upload time. If a file with the same fingerprint already exists, create a new metadata record pointing to the existing object rather than storing a new copy. Reference counting on objects ensures we only delete when the last reference is removed. This is how Dropbox's 'LanSync' and server-side deduplication work.

quiz.question: Why do we use Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) instead of fixed-size chunks for delta sync?
quiz.answer: Fixed-size chunks shift *all* chunk boundaries when a byte is inserted near the start of a file, causing every subsequent chunk to get a new fingerprint. This forces a re-upload of the entire file. CDC uses a rolling hash (like Rabin fingerprinting) to find boundaries based on *content*, so a small edit only affects the 2-3 chunks surrounding the change. A 1-byte edit in a 1GB file might only re-upload ~10MB instead of 1GB.

quiz.question: Why does the File Service verify chunk uploads via S3 ListParts instead of trusting the client's PATCH request?
quiz.answer: Trusting the client to report chunk status is a security risk — a malicious client could mark all chunks as uploaded without actually sending data, leaving a corrupted file entry. By calling S3 ListParts, the server independently verifies which parts actually exist in S3 with valid ETags. This 'trust but verify' approach ensures metadata state always matches storage state.

quiz.question: Why do we need both WebSocket push AND periodic polling for sync? Can't we just use one?
quiz.answer: WebSockets alone fail when devices sleep, switch networks, or lose connectivity — mobile apps are especially prone to this. Polling alone introduces 30+ second latency, which feels broken for real-time collaboration. The hybrid approach gives sub-second updates when online (WebSocket) with a safety net (polling every few minutes) that guarantees no changes are missed even after hours of disconnection.

quiz.question: Why generate CDN-signed URLs with short expiration (5 minutes) instead of long-lived public URLs?
quiz.answer: Signed URLs are bearer tokens — anyone with the URL can download the file. A 5-minute expiration limits the window of exposure if a user accidentally shares a link publicly. For higher security, we can add IP binding or require authentication cookies alongside the signed URL. The tradeoff is that clients must re-request URLs frequently, but this is cheap since URL generation is a purely local cryptographic operation.

quiz.question: Why is client-side compression done before chunking, and why skip it for media files?
quiz.answer: Compression must happen *before* chunking because encryption and many file formats introduce entropy that makes compression ineffective afterward. We skip compression for media files (images, videos, audio) because these formats are already compressed (JPEG, H.264, MP3) — applying gzip or zstd yields <2% size reduction while consuming significant CPU. Text files and code, however, often compress 5-10x, making the CPU cost worthwhile on slower networks.

quiz.question: What happens if the File Service crashes between calling S3 CompleteMultipartUpload and updating the metadata DB to 'uploaded'?
quiz.answer: The file exists in S3 but the metadata still shows 'uploading'. The next time the client polls or the sync service runs a reconciliation job, it detects the mismatch: S3 confirms the object exists but metadata says incomplete. The reconciliation worker updates the metadata to 'uploaded' and emits the change event. Alternatively, S3 event notifications on object creation can trigger an idempotent metadata update.

summary:
### Architecture Overview

This design models a cloud file storage and sync service (Google Drive / Dropbox) built for scale, reliability, and low latency.

### Key Design Principles

**Separate control plane from data plane.** File bytes never flow through our application servers. Clients upload and download directly to/from object storage (S3) and CDN edges using cryptographically signed URLs. Our backend (File Service, Sync Service) only handles metadata, permissions, and coordination — operations that are thousands of times lighter than moving multi-gigabyte files.

**Chunked, resumable, deduplicated uploads.** Files are split into content-defined chunks (CDC) on the client. Each chunk is fingerprinted (SHA-256) for global deduplication — if 1,000 users upload the same PDF, we store it once. Chunking also enables resumable uploads: a 50GB upload interrupted at 49GB only retries the remaining chunks, not the entire file.

**Delta sync for fast synchronization.** When a file changes, CDC ensures only the modified chunks are re-uploaded. A single-byte edit in a 1GB file might only transfer ~10MB. The sync service pushes changes in real-time via WebSocket and falls back to polling for reliability.

**CDN-backed downloads with security.** Downloads are served from 400+ CDN edge locations using signed URLs with short expiration (5 minutes). This minimizes latency for global users while preventing unauthorized link sharing. Range requests enable resumable downloads on flaky mobile networks.

**Normalized permissions model.** Sharing is implemented via a SharedFiles table (userId -> fileId) rather than embedded arrays. This turns 'find files shared with me' from an O(N) table scan into a single efficient query, with Redis caching hot lookups.

### Fault Tolerance

- **Upload crashes:** Metadata reconciliation jobs detect S3 objects that exist but metadata shows 'uploading', and repair the state idempotently.
- **Chunkserver / S3 zone failure:** S3 provides 3x cross-zone replication by default.
- **WebSocket drops:** Polling fallback guarantees eventual consistency.
- **CDN cache corruption:** S3 ETags and checksums validate integrity on every origin fetch.
